Let $r\geq1$, let $H_1=\mathbb C^r$ with ordered orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let
$\mathcal F_-(H_1)=\bigoplus_{k=0}^{r}\bigwedge^k H_1$ be its finite-mode
fermionic Fock space. Let $\mathcal A_r$ be the unital *-algebra generated
by its annihilation and creation operators; it is finite-dimensional. Let
$c_j,c_j^*$ be those operators in this basis, satisfying
$$c_ic_j+c_jc_i=0,\qquad c_ic_j^*+c_j^*c_i=\delta_{ij}I,\qquad c_i^*c_j^*+c_j^*c_i^*=0.$$
A state is a complex-linear functional $\omega$ on $\mathcal A_r$ such that
$\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(X^*X)\geq0$ for every $X\in\mathcal A_r$. Define
the gauge automorphism $\gamma_\theta$ by
$\gamma_\theta(c_j)=e^{-i\theta}c_j$ and
$\gamma_\theta(c_j^*)=e^{i\theta}c_j^*$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R$; the CAR
relations are preserved, so these assignments extend to a one-parameter
family of algebra automorphisms. A state is gauge invariant when
$\omega(\gamma_\theta(X))=\omega(X)$ for every $X$ and every $\theta$.

For a gauge-invariant state, define its one-particle covariance matrix
$C\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ by $C_{ji}:=\omega(c_i^*c_j)$. A finite
gauge-invariant state is quasifree when $C=C^*$, $0\leq C\leq I$, and its
normally ordered moments obey the following rule: for $p\neq q$,
$$\omega(c_{i_1}^*\cdots c_{i_p}^*c_{j_q}\cdots c_{j_1})=0,$$
and for $p=q$,
$$\omega(c_{i_1}^*\cdots c_{i_p}^*c_{j_p}\cdots c_{j_1})=\det\!\left[\omega(c_{i_a}^*c_{j_b})\right]_{a,b=1}^{p}=\det\!\left[C_{j_bi_a}\right]_{a,b=1}^{p}.$$
The empty moment is $\omega(I)=1$. The inequalities $0\leq C\leq I$ mean
$\langle Cv,v\rangle\geq0$ and
$\langle(I-C)v,v\rangle\geq0$ for all $v\in H_1$. Moments of words not
in normal order are obtained by reordering with the displayed CAR relations.

For a Hermitian one-particle matrix $h=h^*$, a real chemical potential $\mu$,
and $\beta>0$, define
$$d\Gamma(h-\mu I):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{r}c_i^*(h-\mu I)_{ij}c_j,\qquad Z:=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(e^{-\beta d\Gamma(h-\mu I)}\right),\qquad \rho:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta d\Gamma(h-\mu I)}.$$
The finite grand Gibbs state has covariance
$$C=(I+e^{\beta(h-\mu I)})^{-1}.$$
Here $h$ and $\mu$ are in joules, $\beta$ is in inverse joules, and $C$ is
dimensionless. The existence and uniqueness of the state for every
Hermitian contraction $C$, and the displayed finite Gibbs covariance formula,
are established by an earlier finite-dimensional result.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix an integer $r\geq1$,
an action scale $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and
the finite-mode Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$. In Schrödinger
coordinates, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ be the Schwartz space
$$\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^r):\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^r}|x^\alpha\partial^\gamma f(x)|<\infty\text{ for every }\alpha,\gamma\in\mathbb N_0^r\}.$$
Here $\mathbb N_0$ denotes the nonnegative integers,
$x^\alpha=\prod_jx_j^{\alpha_j}$, and
$\partial^\gamma=\prod_j\partial_{x_j}^{\gamma_j}$.
Use the dense domain $\mathcal D:=\mathcal U^{-1}\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ and
define on it the operators $Q_j$ and $P_j$ by transporting multiplication
by $\sqrt{\hbar}\,x_j$ and differentiation $-i\sqrt{\hbar}\,\partial_{x_j}$
through $\mathcal U$. Thus, for $f\in\mathcal S$,
$(Q_j\mathcal U^{-1}f)=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt{\hbar}\,x_jf)$ and
$(P_j\mathcal U^{-1}f)=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt{\hbar}\,\partial_{x_j}f)$.
Use the commutator convention $[A,B]=AB-BA$ on common invariant domains.
These quadratures satisfy $[Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I$ on $\mathcal D$
and have units $\sqrt{\mathrm{joule}\cdot\mathrm{second}}$. Each product
Hermite function is a polynomial times a Gaussian; all its derivatives and
polynomial multiples remain a polynomial times that Gaussian and are bounded
on $\mathbb R^r$. Thus the complete product Hermite family lies in
$\mathcal S$, so $\mathcal D$ is dense. The finite-mode Fock-to-Schrödinger
supplier establishes completeness and the quadrature actions used here.
Reorder the quadrature column to grouped order
$R_g:=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)^T$.

A finite positive quadratic canonical operator is specified by a real
symmetric matrix $G\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ with
$x^TGx>0$ for every $x\neq0$, and a real constant $c$. The coefficient
$G$ has units of inverse seconds and $c$ has units of joules. On $\mathcal D$
define the symmetrically ordered operator
$$H_{G,c}^{(0)}:=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}G_{ab}(R_{g,a}R_{g,b}+R_{g,b}R_{g,a})+cI.$$
The real multiplication and derivative operators preserve Schwartz space,
so this finite sum maps $\mathcal D$ into $\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)$.
Integration by parts makes each $Q_j,P_j$ symmetric on $\mathcal D$. For
$f,g\in\mathcal D$, symmetry and invariance of $\mathcal D$ give
$\langle R_{g,a}R_{g,b}f,g\rangle
=\langle R_{g,b}f,R_{g,a}g\rangle
=\langle f,R_{g,b}R_{g,a}g\rangle$; the same identity with $a,b$
interchanged proves that each symmetrized summand is symmetric. Since
$G_{ab}=G_{ba}\in\mathbb R$, the finite sum is symmetric. Its quadratic
coefficients are strictly positive in the stated matrix sense. The statement
does not yet assert that this symmetric operator is self-adjoint.

In grouped coordinates set
$$J_g:=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_\omega:=\operatorname{diag}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r,\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r).$$
A finite diagonalization certificate for $G$ consists of matrices
$U,V\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ and positive angular frequencies $\omega_j>0$ in
inverse seconds such that, with $^*$ denoting conjugate transpose and $^T$
transpose without conjugation,
$$UU^*-VV^*=I_r,\qquad UV^T=VU^T,$$
$$S_g:=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(U+V)&-\operatorname{Im}(U-V)\\\operatorname{Im}(U+V)&\operatorname{Re}(U-V)\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_g^TJ_gS_g=J_g,\qquad S_g^TGS_g=D_\omega.$$
This certificate is explicit finite-dimensional data. No claim is made here
that every positive $G$ has such a certificate; the theorem on this page
uses it as a stated hypothesis. Each term in $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ has units of
joules because $Q_j$ and $P_j$ have units $\sqrt{\mathrm{joule}\cdot\mathrm{second}}$.

A finite diagonalization certificate for $G$ consists of matrices

Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and the finite-mode Fock conventions of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. Let $U,V\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ obey
$$UU^*-VV^*=I_r,\qquad UV^T=VU^T,$$
where $^*$ is conjugate transpose and $^T$ is transpose without conjugation.
On the finite Hermite core define
$$a'_j=\sum_k(U_{jk}a_k+V_{jk}a_k^*).$$
Then the $a'_j$ satisfy $[a'_j,(a'_k)^*]=\delta_{jk}I$ and
$[a'_j,a'_k]=0$ on that core. The real matrix
$$S_g=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(U+V)&-\operatorname{Im}(U-V)\\ \operatorname{Im}(U+V)&\operatorname{Re}(U-V)\end{pmatrix}$$
is symplectic in grouped coordinate order $(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)$.
There is a unitary $M$ on finite-mode Fock, obtained by transporting an
individual finite symplectic implementer through the Fock–Schrödinger
unitary, such that $M^*aM=a'$ on the transported Schwartz core and
$M^*W(z)M=W(S_g^Tz)$ in grouped Weyl-label order. The transformed vacuum
$M\Omega$ has finite mean number
$$\sum_j\|a_jM\Omega\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(VV^*).$$
No infinite-mode implementability assertion is made.

Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and $\hbar>0$. Let $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$,
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
and let $W(z)$ be the regular irreducible Weyl system of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. For every real
$S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$, there is a unitary $M_S$ on
$L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ such that
$$M_S^*W(z)M_S=W(S^Tz)\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r});$$
equivalently, $M_S^*RM_S=SR$ on the common transported Schwartz core.
Any two such implementers differ by a scalar of modulus one. The same
construction applies in every nonzero irreducible regular representation
with this finite phase space and fixed central parameter $\hbar$, after the
unitary equivalence of
[[thm-nrqmx-finite-weyl-uniqueness-interface]].

There is also a connected topological group
$\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ of normalized propagators of real
homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonians on this finite-mode Schrödinger space.
Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism means a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$
whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of the Schwartz space
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ with continuous inverse. A normalized propagator
starts at the identity and solves $i\hbar\,\partial_tU(t)=H_tU(t)$ for a
real symmetrically ordered quadratic $H_t$ with no linear or scalar term.
Give $\operatorname{Mp}$ the topology of pointwise convergence of $U$ and
$U^{-1}$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ in its Schwartz topology; give
$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ its usual matrix topology.
The map
$$\pi:\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R),\qquad M\longmapsto S \quad\text{when }M^*W(z)M=W(S^Tz),$$
is a two-fold covering homomorphism. Its two points over $S$ act by $M_S$
and $-M_S$ when $M_S$ denotes either normalized lift; an arbitrary Weyl
implementer may differ from them by any scalar phase. This connected double
cover and its unitary action are the metaplectic group and metaplectic
representation. All mode counts here are finite; no infinite-mode
implementation claim is part of the statement.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
Here $q_*=0$ by convention when $I$ is empty; for nonempty $I$ the displayed supremum is unchanged. In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be a nonempty open interval. If for every compact $B\subset J$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then throughout $J$, $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a linear
operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$ and graph $\Gamma(T)$
([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

$T$ is **densely defined** when $D(T)$ is a dense subset of $H$
([[def-dense-top]]); **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of
$H\oplus H$; and **closable** when $T$ has a closed extension.
Recall that the graph norm is $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.

**The graph-norm dictionary.** The following three statements are part of the
definition's content and are proved in the remarks below rather than assumed:

1. $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, and
   $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ onto
   $\Gamma(T)$;
2. $T$ is closed if and only if $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
3. if $T$ is closed, then $D(T)$ is a Hilbert space for the inner product
   $\langle x,y\rangle_T=\langle x,y\rangle+\langle Tx,Ty\rangle$ whose induced
   norm is $\|\cdot\|_T$.

A linear subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a **core** for a closed operator $T$
when $D_0$ is dense in $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$, equivalently when
$\overline{\Gamma(T|_{D_0})}=\Gamma(T)$, where the closure is taken in
$H\oplus H$ and $T|_{D_0}$ denotes the restriction of $T$ to $D_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), with Hilbert adjoint $T^*\in\mathcal B(K,H)$
([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]).

**The absolute value.** The operator $T^*T\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact, since it
is the composite of the compact $T$ with the bounded $T^*$
([[lem-compositions-with-a-compact-operator-are-compact]]); it is self-adjoint,
because $(T^*T)^*=T^*T^{**}=T^*T$ ([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]); and it
is positive, because
$$\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\langle Tx,Tx\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\ge0$$
for every $x\in H$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]).
The **absolute value** of $T$ is the unique compact self-adjoint positive
operator
$$|T|:=(T^*T)^{1/2}$$
with $|T|^{2}=T^*T$, whose existence and uniqueness are the preceding square-root
lemma ([[lem-positive-square-root-of-a-compact-positive-operator]]). It satisfies
$$\||T|x\|^{2}=\langle|T|^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\qquad(x\in H),$$
so in particular $\bigl\||T|\bigr\|=\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]) and
$\ker|T|=\ker T$, since $\||T|x\|=\|Tx\|$ for every $x$.

**The singular values.** By the spectral theorem for $|T|$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]]) the nonzero
eigenvalues of $|T|$ form a finite or countably infinite set of positive reals,
each with finite multiplicity, and for every real $\varepsilon>0$ only finitely
many of them exceed $\varepsilon$; positivity rules out negative eigenvalues and
$0$ already corresponds to the kernel. The **multiset of positive singular
values of $T$** is the multiset of positive eigenvalues of $|T|$, counted with
multiplicity ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]).

**The ordered singular-value sequence.** The **distinct** positive singular
values are listed with positive labels in *decreasing* order $\mu_1>\mu_2>\cdots$ as follows:
if the multiset of positive eigenvalues is empty (equivalently $|T|=0$,
equivalently $T=0$), the list is empty; otherwise $\mu_1:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$
is an eigenvalue of $|T|\}$, a maximum and not merely a supremum, because a
supremum value not attained would be an accumulation point different from $0$;
having chosen $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_k$, put $\mu_{k+1}:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$ is an
eigenvalue of $|T|$ and $\lambda<\mu_k\}$ whenever that set is nonempty, and stop
otherwise. Each step is legitimate by the finiteness-above-thresholds property
above, and an infinite list satisfies $\mu_k\to0$ (otherwise its decreasing
limit would be a nonzero accumulation point). Writing $d_k$ for the multiplicity
of $\mu_k$ (a positive integer), the **zero-padded singular-value sequence** is
$$s_1\ge s_2\ge s_3\ge\cdots$$
where $s_1=\cdots=s_{d_1}=\mu_1$, $s_{d_1+1}=\cdots=s_{d_1+d_2}=\mu_2$, and so
on; if the multiset is finite with total multiplicity $r=d_1+\cdots+d_m$, one
sets $s_n:=0$ for every $n>r$, and if $T=0$ one sets $s_n:=0$ for every
$n\ge1$. The number $s_n$ is written $s_n(T)$ and called the $n$-th **singular
value** of $T$.

**Zero-based domain and positive labels.** Set $s_0(T):=\|T\|=s_1(T)$.
Thus the numerical sequence is the function $n\mapsto s_n(T)$ on all of
$\mathbb N$, including zero. The positive-labelled tail $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$
is the multiplicity-counting list constructed above. The auxiliary initial
value $s_0$ is not an additional entry of the eigenvalue multiset, does not index
a singular vector, and is excluded from multiplicity counts and singular-value
sums, which use $n\ge1$. The full sequence satisfies
$s_0\ge s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots$ and tends to zero. This preserves the page's
positive rank labels while giving convergence statements a zero-based domain.

**Rank and the finiteness of the list.** The map $\Phi:\operatorname{ran}|T|\to\operatorname{ran}T$
given by $\Phi(|T|x):=Tx$ is well defined and linear, because $|T|x=|T|x'$ forces
$x-x'\in\ker|T|=\ker T$ and hence $Tx=Tx'$; it is injective, because $Tx=0$ gives
$x\in\ker T=\ker|T|$ and $|T|x=0$; it is surjective onto $\operatorname{ran}T$
because $T=\Phi\circ|T|$; and it is isometric, $\|Tx\|=\||T|x\|$. Hence
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional if and only if
$\operatorname{ran}|T|$ is finite-dimensional; in that case the linear
bijection $\Phi$ gives
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T=\dim\operatorname{ran}|T|$
([[def-dimension]]). Consequently, whenever $T$ has finite rank, the positive
singular values with multiplicity number exactly
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T$, the rank of $T$, and all later $s_n$ vanish, so the
sequence is **zero-padded**. If $T$ does not have finite rank, the multiset of
positive singular values is infinite and countable
([[def-countable]]) and $s_n>0$ for every $n$, with $s_n\downarrow0$; in
particular finite rank of $T$ is characterised by the eventual vanishing $s_n=0$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, and conversely such eventual vanishing forces finite rank. The sequence $(s_n)$ is numerical data only: no orthonormal system is
selected here, and the zero padding is *not* an indexing of any family of
vectors. The unordered multiset determines $(s_n)$ uniquely, so $(s_n)$ is well
defined, and $s_1(T)=\||T|\|=\|T\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint positive operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ is a
nonnegative real for every $x$. Then there is a compact self-adjoint positive
operator $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ with $S^{2}=T$, and it is unique: if
$R\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact and positive
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]) with $R^{2}=T$,
then $R=S$. The root acts by multiplication by $\sqrt\lambda$ on each positive
eigenspace $E_\lambda(T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)$, $\lambda>0$, and by zero on
$\ker T$; in particular $S$ is the operator denoted $\sqrt T$ or $T^{1/2}$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the certificate's matrices give a unitary $M$ satisfying $M^*R_gM=S_gR_g$ on the common transported Schwartz core. By [F3], we may take this implementer to preserve Schwartz space: its normalized metaplectic implementer has that property, and multiplying by a scalar phase leaves $M^*R_gM$ unchanged.

Conjugating each symmetrically ordered term of $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ by $M$ replaces $R_g$ by $S_gR_g$ . Collecting the finite sums gives $$M^*H_{G,c}^{(0)}M=\frac14\sum_{a,b}(S_g^TGS_g)_{ab}(R_{g,a}R_{g,b}+R_{g,b}R_{g,a})+cI.$$ By [A2] this is the diagonal quadratic with coefficient $D_\omega$ on the same core.

On the finite Hermite core put $a_j=(Q_j+iP_j)/\sqrt{2\hbar}$ and $a_j^*=(Q_j-iP_j)/\sqrt{2\hbar}$ . The relation $[Q_j,P_j]=i\hbar I$ gives $Q_j^2+P_j^2=2\hbar(a_j^*a_j+\tfrac12 I)$ by direct multiplication. Consequently the diagonal quadratic is $\sum_j\hbar\omega_j(a_j^*a_j+\tfrac12 I)+cI$ . Write $g_{\mathbf n}\in L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ for the product Hermite basis and set $\phi_{\mathbf n}:=\mathcal U^{-1}g_{\mathbf n}\in\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)$ . Then $\mathcal U\phi_{\mathbf n}=g_{\mathbf n}$ , and the diagonal quadratic has eigenvalue $E_{\mathbf n}=c+\sum_j\hbar\omega_j(n_j+\tfrac12)$ . Denote this diagonal differential expression on $\mathcal S$ by $\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}$ , and its Fock-space transport on $\mathcal D$ by $T_\omega^{(0)}:=\mathcal U^{-1}\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}\mathcal U$ .

Put $\epsilon_j=\hbar\omega_j$ and let $A$ be the maximal diagonal multiplier in the basis $(\phi_{\mathbf n})$ with eigenvalues $\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j$ . By [F5], $A$ is self-adjoint on the domain where $\sum_{\mathbf n}|\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j|^2|f_{\mathbf n}|^2<\infty$ . The diagonal operator with eigenvalues $E_{\mathbf n}$ is $A+c_0I$ , where $c_0=c+\tfrac12\sum_j\epsilon_j$ . Its domain is the same: for real $x,c_0$ , $|x+c_0|^2\leq2|x|^2+2|c_0|^2$ and $|x|^2\leq2|x+c_0|^2+2|c_0|^2$ , and each coefficient sequence $(f_{\mathbf n})$ is in $\ell^2$ . For $g\in D((A+c_0I)^*)$ , [F7] says that boundedness of $f\mapsto\langle(A+c_0I)f,g\rangle$ and boundedness of $f\mapsto c_0\langle f,g\rangle$ imply boundedness of $f\mapsto\langle Af,g\rangle$ . Thus $g\in D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $(A+c_0I)^*g=Ag+c_0g$ . Conversely, every $g\in D(A)$ satisfies this adjoint identity, so $T=A+c_0I$ is self-adjoint. Finite Hermite truncations converge in its graph norm, because the tail of $\sum_{\mathbf n}(1+|E_{\mathbf n}|^2)|f_{\mathbf n}|^2$ tends to zero. Thus finite Hermite sums are a core for $T$ in the graph norm of [F8].

For $\psi\in\mathcal D$ , put $f=\mathcal U\psi\in\mathcal S$ . The coordinate expression $\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}$ sends $f$ to an $L^2$ function. Integration by parts against each Schwartz Hermite function gives $\langle T_\omega^{(0)}\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle =E_{\mathbf n}\langle\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle$ ; equivalently, this is the $L^2$ pairing of the differential expression on $f$ with $g_{\mathbf n}=\mathcal U\phi_{\mathbf n}$ . Boundary terms vanish because both functions are Schwartz. For every finite set $F$ of occupation indices, orthogonal projection therefore gives $\sum_{\mathbf n\in F}|E_{\mathbf n}\langle\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2 \leq\|T_\omega^{(0)}\psi\|^2$ . These coefficients are square-summable, and completeness of $(\phi_{\mathbf n})$ from [F4] identifies their vector with $T_\omega^{(0)}\psi$ . Hence $\mathcal D\subseteq D(T)$ and the diagonal expression is $T$ on $\mathcal D$ . The finite Hermite sums from step 4.1 lie in $\mathcal D$ because [F1] places each $g_{\mathbf n}$ in $\mathcal S$ , and are graph-norm dense in $D(T)$ ; so the graph closure of this restriction is $T$.

By step 1.1, $M$ and $M^*$ preserve Schwartz space, and by step 2.1 $H_{G,c}^{(0)}=M T_\omega^{(0)}M^*$ there. Step 5.1 gives graph closure $T$ for the diagonal restriction. Conjugation by the unitary $M$ carries the graph and its closure in $\mathcal F_s\oplus\mathcal F_s$ to the graph and closure of $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ , so $H=\overline{H_{G,c}^{(0)}}=MTM^*$ . This is self-adjoint because $T$ is self-adjoint and $M$ is unitary.

Set $q_j=e^{-\beta\epsilon_j}=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j}$ . Since $\beta>0$ and every $\omega_j>0$ , $0<q_j<1$ ; the mode set is finite, so $q_*<1$ and $\sum_jq_j<\infty$ . Apply [F5] to the diagonal number-energy operator $A$ to get $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty$ . On the occupation basis, $T$ has eigenvalues $E_{\mathbf n}=c_0+\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j$ , so the spectral exponential has positive eigenvalues $e^{-\beta E_{\mathbf n}}=e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_jq_j^{n_j}$ by [F9]. Thus $e^{-\beta T}=e^{-\beta c_0}e^{-\beta A}$ on the occupation basis; [F10] and the trace-class conclusion for $e^{-\beta A}$ from [F5] show that $e^{-\beta T}$ is positive trace class. Its eigenvalue sum is $e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty$ by [F5], so [F6] identifies that sum with its trace. By steps 6.1 and 5.1, the vectors $M\phi_{\mathbf n}$ form a complete orthonormal eigenbasis for $H$ with the same eigenvalues; equivalently $e^{-\beta H}=M e^{-\beta T}M^*$ . The unitary invariance in [F10] makes $e^{-\beta H}$ trace class with the same eigenvalue sum, and [F6] gives the same trace. Finally, $$e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_j(1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j})^{-1}=e^{-\beta c}\prod_j\frac{e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j/2}}{1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j}}=e^{-\beta c}\prod_j\left[2\sinh\!\left(\frac{\beta\hbar\omega_j}{2}\right)\right]^{-1}.$$ Every factor is strictly positive and finite, proving $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$ . The only infinite-dimensional Hilbert space used here is the bosonic Fock space for the stated finite number $r$ of modes.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $r\geq1$,
$\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $\beta>0$ in inverse joules, $c\in\mathbb R$ in
joules, and let $G=G^T$ be a strictly positive real $2r\times2r$ matrix
whose entries have units of inverse seconds. Assume $(U,V,\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r)$
is a finite diagonalization certificate for $G$ as defined earlier, with
each $\omega_j>0$ in inverse seconds. Let $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ be the symmetric
quadratic operator on the stated Schwartz domain. Then its graph closure
$H:=\overline{H_{G,c}^{(0)}}$ exists and is self-adjoint, and its finite-mode
Gibbs partition sum is
$$Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})=e^{-\beta c}\prod_{j=1}^{r}\left[2\sinh\!\left(\frac{\beta\hbar\omega_j}{2}\right)\right]^{-1}\in(0,\infty),\qquad \sinh x:=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{2}.$$
The matrix $G$ acts on the finite grouped quadratures; the bosonic Fock
space remains infinite-dimensional at each $r\geq1$. This conditional
finite-mode conclusion neither proves that every positive $G$ has a
diagonalization certificate nor asserts infinite-mode implementability,
interacting depletion bounds, or superfluidity.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
Here $q_*=0$ by convention when $I$ is empty; for nonempty $I$ the displayed supremum is unchanged. In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be a nonempty open interval. If for every compact $B\subset J$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then throughout $J$, $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to the reduced finite mode set $\{2,\ldots,r\}$ with $\epsilon_k=\hbar\omega_k$ . Its factors satisfy $q_k=e^{-\beta\epsilon_k}\in(0,1)$ , and the set is finite, so the hypotheses $q_*<1$ and $\sum_{k=2}^rq_k<\infty$ hold. Its occupation partition sum is $\prod_{k=2}^{r}(1-q_k)^{-1}$ ; adding each oscillator's zero-point energy $\hbar\omega_k/2$ multiplies this by $e^{-\beta\sum_{k=2}^r\hbar\omega_k/2}$ , giving $\prod_{k=2}^{r}[2\sinh(\beta\hbar\omega_k/2)]^{-1}$ . If $r=1$ , the reduced set is empty and its sum and product are both $1$ .

For each $k\geq2$ , put $x_k=\beta\hbar\omega_k>0$ . Its one-mode occupation sum is $$\sum_{n_k=0}^{\infty}e^{-x_k(n_k+1/2)}=\frac{e^{-x_k/2}}{1-e^{-x_k}}=\left[2\sinh(x_k/2)\right]^{-1},$$ which is positive and finite. If the first occupation is restricted to $0\leq n_1\leq N$ and the remaining modes are summed, the resulting partial sum is $$(N+1)\prod_{k=2}^{r}\left[2\sinh(x_k/2)\right]^{-1}.$$ This tends to $+\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ ; when $r=1$ the product is empty and the same partial sum is $N+1$ . Hence $Z_\beta=+\infty$ .

Removing mode $1$ changes the occupation Hilbert space and leaves only the finite product over $k\geq2$ . The full system has an additional countably infinite zero-energy occupation degeneracy, so its positive Gibbs weights cannot be normalized. The finite positive-frequency theorem does not apply at $\omega_1=0$ , and the omitted-mode product is the partition sum of a different model.
